blocks.content: A container's writable layer is disposable, it disappears the moment the container is removed. Volumes exist to give data a place to live that survives independently of any one container's lifecycle.
1. The Problem: Writable Layers Do Not Survive
blocks.text: 1. The Problem: Writable Layers Do Not Survive

blocks.content: As covered in the Docker Containers module, everything a container writes normally lands in its own writable layer, and that layer is deleted the instant the container is removed. For a stateless web server that is fine, for a database, that is catastrophic.

blocks.alt: The writable layer, and everything in it, disappears on removal

blocks.content: 2. Volumes Live Independently of Any Container
blocks.text: 2. Volumes Live Independently of Any Container

blocks.content: A volume is storage Docker manages separately from any specific container's lifecycle. A container mounts a volume to read and write through it, but removing that container does not touch the volume's data at all.

blocks.alt: A volume outlives the container that used it

blocks.content: 3. The Same Data, Across a New Container
blocks.text: 3. The Same Data, Across a New Container

blocks.content: This is exactly what makes recreating a container safe: stop the old one, start a new one (perhaps from an updated image), mount the same volume, and the data is exactly where it left off, as if nothing happened to it.

blocks.alt: The old container is gone, the volume and its data are not

blocks.content: This is why every real database container (Postgres, MySQL, MongoDB, and the rest) is run with its data directory mounted as a volume, upgrading the database image, restarting the container, even accidentally removing and recreating it, none of that touches the actual data.

blocks.alt: The data survives everything that happens to the container itself

blocks.content:
docker run -d -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres
# Even if this container is removed and a new one started with
# the same volume, the database data is exactly as it was.

code.content:
docker run -d -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres
# Even if this container is removed and a new one started with
# the same volume, the database data is exactly as it was.

codes.bash:
docker run -d -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres
# Even if this container is removed and a new one started with
# the same volume, the database data is exactly as it was.

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: A container's writable layer is disposable, volumes exist specifically to give data a lifecycle independent of any one container.
Any stateful workload, most obviously a database, should have its data directory mounted as a volume, not left in the writable layer.
